newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arthuis says no compromise on French pension funds.
newsitem.headline: Arthuis says no compromise on French pension funds.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis on Tuesday ruled out any compromise with unions over plans to introduce pension funds to France.

Trade union leaders on Monday slammed a government pension funds bill, due to be given a second reading in parliament later on Tuesday, saying it would drain money from the existing universal pension system.
The bill will exempt employer contributions to pension funds from payroll charges, which are used to fund the welfare and pensions system.
Asked whether there was any possibility of reaching a compromise with unions on the pension funds, Arthuis told Reuters "absolutely not".
He denied the pension funds would damage the traditional pay-as-you-go or "distribution" retirement benefit system.
"Retirement savings funds are not going to cannibalise our pensions via distribution," he told a conference.
"On the contrary, by strengthening our companies, they will encourage the creation of wealth and jobs and, therefore, increase the resources of the basic system in the medium and long-term."
The aim was to give workers and companies the option to create another level of pensions, government spokesman Alain Lamassoure told French radio.
"There is no risk that the development of pension funds will be to the detriment of the distribution system which remains the fundamental element of our retirement system," he said.

The government has said the pension funds, which operate on a system of capitalisation whereby people save themselves for their pensions, will complement the distribution system under which pensioners are paid out of payroll charges on today's workforce.
It hopes the pension funds will also boost the stock market and help channel resources into equities.
They will be set up under voluntary agreements between companies and their employees and will be given tax benefits.
The plans are part of an overall tax reform designed to funnel French savings into productive investment, thereby fuelling growth and helping to bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment.
Until the recent reduction in interest rates, most savings went largely to money market funds, dubbed "sleeping money" by the government.
"Our ambition is to create the economic, fiscal and regulatory framework which will allow the best allocation of resources for the benefit of activity and employment," Arthuis told the conference.
Unions, however, fear the introduction of pension funds may be the first step in a run-down of the deficit-burdened welfare system, which covers healthcare, pensions and family benefits.
The National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, was due to start debating pension funds at around 1600 GMT and vote on the bill either late on Tuesday or early on Wednesday.
The bill was then due to go back to the Senate, the upper house of parliament, for a second reading.
